* Keep a diary of their daily step counts
* Learn to assess their own physical fatigue and mental fatigue level during boxing exercise sessions.
title: Impact of Community-based Boxing Exercises in Individuals With Chronic Stroke

brief_summary: Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) is a leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide, placing a substantial burden on healthcare systems and society.1 Despite intensive advancements in the stroke care, incomplete neurological recovery after stroke is quite common, with many survivors experiencing persistent motor, cognitive, or sensory deficits.2 These long-term impairments significantly affect the quality of life and highlight the need for additional neurorestorative therapies.3,4 The pathophysiology of ischemic stroke involves a complex cascade of events including excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis, which contribute to neuronal injury and limit functional recovery.5,6 Current treatment strategies primarily focus on revascularization and supportive care, with limited options available to actively promote neuroprotection and regeneration.7,8 Melatonin, an endogenous neurohormone hormone primarily involved in regulating sleep-wake cycles, has been shown to possess several potential therapeutic properties, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective effects.9 These properties have led to investigate the use of melatonin as an adjunctive treatment for various conditions, including stroke.10,11 However, its potential benefit in recovery of neurological status in patients with acute ischemic stroke remains understudied.12 Pre-clinical studies have demonstrated that melatonin can attenuate ischemia-induced brain injury, reduce infarct size, and improve functional outcomes.13 There is a compelling need to explore novel therapeutic interventions that can target neurological recovery in stroke patients. Exogenous melatonin administration offers a promising avenue for this intervention.14, 15 Preliminary studies have shown that melatonin may protect against acute ischemic stroke by suppressing both inflammatory and oxidative stresses.16 The purpose of this study is to evaluate the effects of exogenous melatonin supplementation on the neurological and functional recovery in patients with acute ischemic stroke, potentially leading to improved clinical outcomes. By addressing this research gap, the study seeks to provide valuable insights into the potential role of melatonin as a therapeutic agent in the management of acute ischemic stroke.
title: Melatonin in Stroke

brief_summary: Non-pharmacological methods used to reduce a patient's pain after surgery are important complementary approaches that allow pain to be managed without the potential side effects of medications. Controlling pain in the postoperative period reduces pain-related anxiety in patients, prevents adverse outcomes, facilitates early mobilization, and increases patient comfort and satisfaction, thereby reducing the risk of postoperative complications. It also accelerates recovery, shortens the length of hospital stay, and reduces hospital costs. For these reasons, the use of non-pharmacological pain management following surgical procedures yields positive outcomes for the patient. No study has been found in the literature that measures the effect of cold application-one of the non-pharmacological methods used to alleviate pain in patients following laparoscopic cholecystectomy-on patients' sleep quality and quality of recovery. For this reason, this study is designed to determine the effects of cold therapy applied to the trocar incision site following laparoscopic cholecystectomy on pain, sleep quality, and the quality of postoperative recovery.

brief_summary:
Study Summary: Peanuts, Stress, Sleep, and Cognitive Function

Stress can affect how one thinks, concentrates, and performs everyday mental tasks. Diet may be one factor that influences cognitive function and the body's response to stress, but more research is needed to understand whether specific foods can support brain health and mental well-being.

This study will investigate whether eating peanuts daily for eight weeks influences cognitive function, stress, and sleep in young adults who experience higher levels of daily stress. Researchers are particularly interested in understanding whether regular peanut consumption may influence how the brain responds to challenging tasks and how individuals perform on measures of cognitive function.

Throughout the study, participants will complete assessments of their cognitive function, stress, and well-being. They will wear a wrist-worn device to monitor sleep patterns, heart rate, and daily activity and use a mobile app to complete daily brief questions on their current well-being. During study visits, participants will wear a comfortable, noninvasive device on their forehead that measures changes in blood flow in the brain while they complete tasks designed to assess cognitive function and responses to stress. Saliva samples will also be collected to measure biological markers associated with the body's stress response.

By examining brain activity alongside measures of cognition, sleep, and stress, researchers hope to better understand the relationship between peanut consumption and brain health. This research may help clarify whether incorporating peanuts into the daily diet could influence cognitive performance and other aspects of mental well-being.
primary_outcomes: Cognitive Performance During the Digit Span Task
Cognitive Performance During the Spatial Recall Task
Cognitive Performance During the Symbol Digit Substitution Task
Cognitive Performance During the Trail Making Task
title: The Impact of Peanuts on Brain Function in Young Adults

Motor imagery (MI), the mental simulation of a movement without overt execution, may enhance voluntary muscle activation and sensorimotor awareness.

This pilot randomized controlled trial compared the immediate effects of a single session of PFM-specific MI versus non-specific sit-to-stand MI on PFM maximal voluntary contraction, accessory muscle involvement, and MI quality in postmenopausal women with SUI.

Thirty postmenopausal women with SUI were randomly allocated to one of the two MI groups. Each participant attended one session of about 90 minutes, which included two guided MI sets with three actual maximal voluntary PFM contractions performed between them. PFM maximal voluntary contraction (Modified Oxford Scale), accessory muscle involvement, and MI quality were assessed before and after MI practice.
primary_outcomes: Change in pelvic floor muscle maximal voluntary contraction
Change in accessory muscle involvement during pelvic floor muscle contraction

brief_summary:
Background: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the tooth-supporting tissues, resulting from an imbalance between the host immune response and periodontopathogenic bacteria. Minimally invasive non-surgical therapy (MINST) reduces soft-tissue trauma and preserves clot stability. Healing may be further enhanced by two adjuncts: high-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid (HA), which has anti-inflammatory and mucoadhesive properties, and concentrated growth factor (CGF), an autologous platelet concentrate. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) serves as a marker of inflammation, angiogenesis and healing.

Aim: This study evaluated the clinical and biochemical outcomes of 0.8% HA gel and liquid CGF as adjuncts to MINST in stage II-III periodontitis. The primary outcome was clinical attachment level (CAL) gain at 6 months. Secondary outcomes were probing depth (PD), bleeding on probing (BoP), gingival index (GI), plaque index (PI) and GCF VEGF levels at 1, 3 and 6 months.

Subjects and Methods: This three-arm, parallel-group randomized clinical trial included 66 systemically healthy non-smokers aged 20-40 years with stage II-III periodontitis and pockets of at least 5 mm. Patients were recruited at the Faculty of Dentistry, October 6 University, under ethics approval RECO6U/34-2023. A sample size of 22 per group was calculated with G\*Power (α = 0.05, power 80%, effect size 0.4). After an initial hygiene phase, patients whose full-mouth plaque and bleeding scores fell below 20% were randomized by computer-generated sequence into three groups. Group I received MINST alone. Group II received MINST plus 0.8% HA gel injected subgingivally and repeated after 4 weeks. Group III received MINST plus liquid CGF, prepared from about 9 mL of the patient's venous blood, injected subgingivally and repeated after 4 weeks. MINST was performed under local anesthesia with 5× loupes and Gracey Mini Five curettes, without irrigation. The deepest interproximal site in each patient served as the experimental site. A single calibrated, blinded examiner recorded the clinical parameters at baseline, 1, 3 and 6 months. GCF was collected with paper points, and VEGF was measured by ELISA. CAL, PD and VEGF were analyzed by mixed MANOVA with Bonferroni correction. PI and GI were analyzed with the Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney, Friedman and Wilcoxon tests, and BoP with the chi-square, Cochran's Q and McNemar tests.

Results: All 66 patients completed follow-up. The groups were comparable at baseline (p \> 0.05), and all improved significantly over time (p \< 0.001).

Mean baseline CAL was similar in Groups I, II and III (5.36, 5.41 and 5.32 mm). At 6 months it had fallen to 3.86, 3.36 and 3.05 mm, giving mean gains of 1.50, 2.05 and 2.27 mm respectively. Both adjunct groups gained more attachment than the control from the first month onward, and CGF gained more than HA at 3 and 6 months (p = 0.03).

Mean PD fell from 5.50, 5.36 and 5.41 mm at baseline to 3.82, 3.41 and 2.95 mm at 6 months, reductions of 1.68, 1.95 and 2.46 mm. CGF gave a greater PD reduction than HA at 3 months (p = 0.01) and 6 months (p = 0.002).

GCF VEGF started at similar levels in all groups (about 1790-1820 pg/mL) and fell significantly at every interval. At 6 months it was 1341.40 pg/mL in Group I, 1264.82 pg/mL in Group II and 1182.66 pg/mL in Group III. The CGF group had the lowest levels at 3 and 6 months compared with HA (p = 0.01) and control (p = 0.001).

PI and GI improved in all groups; PI was significantly better with CGF at 3 and 6 months, and GI with CGF at 3 months (p = 0.001), with no GI difference between groups at 6 months.

BoP was present in 20 of 22 patients (90.9%) in each group at baseline. At 1 month it was present in 54.5%, 31.8% and 13.6% of patients in Groups I, II and III (p = 0.016), and in no patient at 3 and 6 months.

Limitations: The study was carried out at a single centre, with a 6-month follow-up and one experimental site per patient. No radiographic or histological assessment was performed, so CAL gain reflects clinical repair through a long junctional epithelium rather than proven regeneration. The control group received no placebo, so the greater PI improvement in the adjunct groups may reflect performance bias. VEGF was first resampled at 1 month, after the early growth-factor release from CGF. Only healthy non-smokers aged 20-40 years were included.

Conclusion: Adding HA gel or liquid CGF to MINST produced greater clinical and biochemical improvement than MINST alone over 6 months in stage II-III periodontitis. CGF was the most effective adjunct for CAL gain, PD reduction and lowering GCF VEGF.
title: Evaluation of Hyaluronic Acid Gel and Concentrated Growth Factor in Periodontal Therapy

brief_summary:
This randomized controlled trial aims to evaluate the effectiveness of wearable technology-supported gamification in reducing pain and anxiety and its effects on heart rate in children aged 6-12 years undergoing venous blood sampling or peripheral intravenous catheterization.

Medical procedures may cause pain, fear, and anxiety in children and can affect their cooperation during treatment. Distraction through age-appropriate digital activities may help children cope with these experiences. This study will investigate whether combining a smart wristband with an interactive digital storytelling activity is more effective than standard care in reducing pain and anxiety during medical procedures.

A total of 60 children will be included in the study, with 30 children assigned to the intervention group and 30 to the control group. Group allocation will be performed using a randomization procedure involving sealed envelopes containing group assignment cards.

Children in the intervention group will wear a smart wristband and participate in an interactive, space-themed digital storytelling activity presented on a tablet. The activity will include age-appropriate story elements and simple interactive tasks, such as touching targets or popping balloons, to redirect children's attention during the procedure. The story will guide children through different stages of the activity, from the beginning of the mission to its completion. At the end of the procedure, children will receive a positive reinforcement sticker. Children in the control group will receive standard nursing care without the gamification intervention.

Pain will be assessed using the Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale, and anxiety will be evaluated using the Modified Yale Preoperative Anxiety Scale. Heart rate will be recorded before, during, and after the procedure. The outcomes will be compared between the intervention and control groups.

The study hypothesis is that wearable technology-supported gamification will be associated with lower pain and anxiety levels and lower heart rates during invasive medical procedures compared with standard care. The study will also examine whether this approach may help improve children's cooperation during the procedures.
primary_outcomes: Pain Intensity Measured by the Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale
Anxiety Level Measured by the Modified Yale Preoperative Anxiety Scale (mYPAS)
title: The Effectiveness of Wearable Technology-Supported Gamification in Reducing Pain and Anxiety During Medical Procedures in Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial

brief_summary:
This study aims to investigate the acute effects of whole-body vibration (WBV) and passive recovery on heart rate variability (HRV) following high-intensity intermittent exercise in male soccer players.

Ten male soccer players will participate in a randomized, two-period crossover study. Each participant will complete two experimental sessions separated by a seven-day washout period. During each session, participants will perform the Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1 until exhaustion, followed by either 15 minutes of seated whole-body vibration or 15 minutes of seated passive recovery.

During the WBV condition, participants will remain seated with their knees flexed at approximately 90 degrees and their bare feet positioned on a vibration platform operating at 35 Hz with a peak-to-peak amplitude of 2 mm. During passive recovery, participants will remain seated without vibration.

Heart rate variability will be continuously recorded throughout the exercise test and the entire 15-minute recovery period using a chest-strap heart rate sensor. Frequency-domain HRV parameters, including very-low-frequency (VLF), low-frequency (LF), and high-frequency (HF) power, will be analyzed.

The study will compare the autonomic responses associated with the two recovery methods to determine whether seated whole-body vibration produces different short-term HRV responses compared with passive recovery.
title: Effects of Whole-Body Vibration on Heart Rate Variability During Post-Exercise Recovery

brief_summary:
People living with severe mental illness (SMI) experience substantial physical health inequalities, including an increased prevalence of cardiovascular disease, obesity, metabolic disorders, reduced physical fitness, and premature mortality. Physical inactivity, prolonged sedentary behavior, sleep disturbances, and the metabolic effects of psychiatric medications may contribute to these health problems.

The PHASMI study aims to provide a comprehensive assessment of physical health, cardiorespiratory fitness, cardiometabolic risk, physical functioning, lifestyle characteristics, emotional well-being, and health-related quality of life in adults with severe mental illness.

The primary objective is to investigate associations between sociodemographic, clinical, and lifestyle characteristics and cardiorespiratory fitness, assessed through peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak).

PHASMI is an observational, descriptive, cross-sectional study conducted in Álava, Spain. The anticipated sample comprises 275 adults aged 18 to 65 years with a diagnosis of severe mental illness according to DSM-5 criteria established by psychiatry specialists. Participants will be recruited through the Mental Health Network of Álava, including individuals receiving community-based psychiatric care and hospitalized patients.

Participants will undergo a comprehensive health assessment involving cardiopulmonary exercise testing on a treadmill using a modified Bruce protocol, the Modified Shuttle Walk Test, anthropometric measurements, body composition analysis, blood pressure measurements, electrocardiography, laboratory analyses, handgrip strength testing, and standardized assessments of physical functioning.

Physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep will be assessed using standardized questionnaires and a wrist-worn ActiGraph GT3X+ accelerometer over eight consecutive days. Emotional well-being and health-related quality of life will be evaluated using validated questionnaires.

The main in-person assessments will be conducted over two consecutive days at the University of the Basque Country and the Psychiatric Hospital of Álava. Written informed consent will be obtained before participation.

No experimental treatment or therapeutic intervention will be assigned. By examining associations between physical fitness, cardiometabolic health, lifestyle characteristics, and psychological well-being, PHASMI seeks to identify potentially modifiable factors associated with poorer physical health and inform future prevention and health promotion strategies for people living with severe mental illness.
primary_outcomes: Peak Oxygen Uptake (VO2peak) Assessed by Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing
title: Health Assessment in People With Severe Mental Illness

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to evaluate whether Parents of Little Ones® - Baby Version®, a self-guided online parenting program, can reduce parenting stress and improve mindful parenting among mothers during the first 12 months after childbirth.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does participation in the program reduce parenting stress?
* Does participation in the program improve mindful parenting?
* Are any improvements in parenting stress and mindful parenting maintained three months after the intervention ends?

Researchers will compare mothers who receive access to the self-guided online program with mothers assigned to a waitlist control group to determine whether the program leads to greater reductions in parenting stress and improvements in mindful parenting, both immediately after the intervention and three months later.

Participants will:

* Complete online questionnaires at three assessment points: before the intervention (baseline), after the intervention period (post-intervention), and three months after the intervention ends (follow-up). These questionnaires will assess parenting stress, mindful parenting, psychological well-being, and other parenting-related outcomes.
* Be randomly assigned to either the intervention group or the waitlist control group.
* If assigned to the intervention group, complete eight self-guided online sessions, preferably one per week, including psychoeducational videos, interactive exercises, mindfulness and self-compassion practices, and activities to apply the strategies in everyday parenting.
* If assigned to the waitlist control group, continue their usual activities without receiving access to the program during the study period.
interventions: Parents of Little Ones - Baby Version (Self-Guided Online Program)
primary_outcomes: Changes in Parenting Stress From Baseline (week 0) to Post-Intervention (up to week 10) and 3-Month Follow-Up (up to week 22)
Changes in Mindful Parenting From Baseline (week 0) to Post-Intervention (up to week 10) and 3-Month Follow-Up (up to week 22)
title: Effects of the Parents of Little Ones® - Baby Version® on Parenting Stress and Mindful Parenting in Postpartum Mothers

brief_summary:
Study LTS18002 is a global, multicenter, open-label (OL), Phase 3, long-term safety and efficacy extension study.

The purpose of this study is to provide continued access to frexalimab for participants with MS, and to evaluate the long-term safety and efficacy profile of frexalimab. This study will monitor delayed AEs, assess the durability of safety findings and characterize any emerging safety signals that may develop over an extended follow up period.

Study details include:

* The study duration will be up to 4 years.
* The OL treatment duration will be up to 96 weeks (corresponding to approximately 2 years) per participant.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis, and liver metastasis is a major contributor to treatment failure and reduced survival. Due to the complex mechanisms underlying tumor progression and metastasis, effective early diagnostic biomarkers and targeted therapeutic strategies remain limited. This study aims to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying PDAC progression and liver metastasis, identify potential biomarkers for early risk prediction and prognostic assessment, and explore novel therapeutic targets to facilitate precision diagnosis and treatment.

Participants will be required to:

* Provide histopathologically confirmed primary PDAC tissue and liver metastatic tissue, together with the corresponding adjacent non-tumor pancreatic tissue
* Undergo regular follow-up visits for monitoring and data collection.
* Allow access to their medical records for relevant clinical information.

brief_summary: This study is being done to determine whether an assay called LymphDetect™ Head and Neck is a useful tool to help guide treatment decisions for patients with head and neck cancer. The LymphDetect™ assay works to detect a certain kind of DNA that is released by tumors called circulating tumor DNA or ctDNA for short. In this study, the presence of ctDNA will be assessed in fluid collected from the surgical drain that will be placed during curative-intent surgical procedure performed as a part of patient standard care. Treatment after surgery is determined by a patient's disease risk category (low-risk, intermediate-risk, or high-risk). Having intermediate-risk with detection of ctDNA in the surgical drain fluid (SDF+) may mean that a patient is at greater risk of their cancer coming back. To reduce this risk, treatment will be more intensive than if ctDNA in the surgical drain fluid (SDF-) was not found.
interventions: Intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) or Intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT)

brief_summary:
Background: Chronic neck pain is associated with pain, functional disability, restricted cervical mobility, and impaired upper-extremity function. Neural mobilization is a manual therapy approach intended to address altered neural mechanosensitivity and improve the mechanical and physiological behavior of peripheral neural tissues. However, its additional effects when combined with conventional physiotherapy in individuals with chronic neck pain remain unclear.

Methods: This study was designed as a single-centre, two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. Participants with chronic neck pain were randomly allocated to either a neural mobilization group or a conventional physiotherapy group. Both groups received a 4-week conventional physiotherapy program consisting of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, therapeutic ultrasound, hot-pack application, and therapeutic neck exercises. Participants allocated to the neural mobilization group additionally received bilateral neural mobilization targeting the median, radial, and ulnar nerves. Treatment was administered over 12 sessions, with three sessions per week.

Outcome Measures: The primary outcomes were activity-related pain, resting pain, and night-time pain, all assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS). These three pain measures were considered equally important primary outcomes. Secondary outcomes included neck-related disability assessed using the Neck Disability Index (NDI), upper-extremity function assessed using the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) questionnaire, and cervical range of motion. Upper-limb neurodynamic test responses were evaluated as exploratory outcomes. Assessments were performed at baseline and immediately after completion of the 4-week intervention.

Objective: The primary objective was to investigate whether adding neural mobilization to conventional physiotherapy provides additional benefits in reducing activity-related, resting, and night-time pain in individuals with chronic neck pain. Secondary objectives were to evaluate its effects on neck-related disability, upper-extremity function, and cervical range of motion. Exploratory analyses also examined changes in upper-limb neurodynamic test responses.
primary_outcomes: Change in Pain Intensity Measured by the Visual Analog Scale (VAS)
title: Effects of Neural Mobilization Added to Conventional Physiotherapy in Chronic Neck Pain

brief_summary:
The fosfomycin-trometamol (FT) combination demonstrates microbiological efficacy against the vast majority of Escherichia coli strains responsible for urinary tract infections (UTIs). Moreover, approximately 99% of strains exhibiting multidrug resistance remain suceptible to fosfomycin.

The clinical tolerance profile of this molecule is excellent and has been well established since its market authorization in 1989 for the treatment of cystitis in women.

Its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties are compatible with its use in the treatment of UTIs in men.

However, the clinical efficacy of FT (oral fosfomycin) in the treatment of febrile UTIs in men has never been evaluated in prospective trials. FT could represent an innovative treatment option in such cases, offering the use if an antibiotic with significantly fewer side effects than those currently recommended.

The main objective of the trial is to demonstrate that FT is not inferior to fluoroquinolones (FQ) or cotrimoxazole (TMP-SMX) as oral step-down therapy in prostatitisfebrile male urinary tract infections caused by Escherichia coli.
title: Randomized, Multicenter, Non-inferiority Trial Comparing the Efficacy of Fosfomycin Versus Fluoroquinolones or Cotrimoxazole as Oral Follow-up Treatment in Febrile Urinary Tract Infections in Men Caused by Susceptible Enterobacteria

brief_summary:
Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is the most common entrapment neuropathy, characterized by the compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. Routine electroneuromyography (ENMG) assesses only thick, myelinated fibers; it fails to account for damage to small, unmyelinated fibers or biomechanical variations within muscle tissue. The objective of this study is to examine-using quantitative methods-the biomechanical parameters (muscle tone, stiffness, and elasticity) of the thenar muscle (abductor pollicis brevis, APB) and cutaneous thermal sensory thresholds in individuals diagnosed with mild or moderate CTS (via EMG) and in healthy controls. Furthermore, the study aims to investigate the relationships between these findings and ultrasonographic nerve cross-sectional area (CSA), grip strength, and clinical assessment scales.

This cross-sectional, prospective study included 43 participants: 15 with mild CTS, 14 with moderate CTS (both confirmed by ENMG), and 14 healthy controls. APB muscle biomechanics were assessed using myotonometry, while thermal sensory thresholds-cold detection threshold (CDT), warm detection threshold (WDT), cold pain threshold (CPT), and heat pain threshold (HPT)-were evaluated using a quantitative sensory testing device. The CSA of the median nerve was measured via ultrasonography at the level of the pisiform bone. Clinical assessment included grip/pinch strength, the Semmes-Weinstein monofilament test, two-point discrimination, the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS), the Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire (BCTSQ), the CTS-6 scale, and the Leeds Assessment of Neuropathic Symptoms and Signs (LANSS) scale. Statistical analyses for intergroup comparisons involved ANOVA, the Kruskal-Wallis test, ANCOVA (with BMI and age as covariates), and post-hoc tests. ROC analysis will be applied for diagnostic performance.
title: Evaluation of Thenar Muscle Biomechanics and Thermal Sensory Thresholds in Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

brief_summary: Recommendations regarding tourniquet use in arteriovenous fistula (AVF) cannulation vary across guidelines. In general, the use of a tourniquet is recommended for all needle insertions into an AVF unless the fistula is aneurysmal. In contrast, tourniquets are not required for arteriovenous grafts. A tourniquet should be applied to assess vessel depth and direction in order to guide needle insertion. However, prolonged application must be avoided to prevent thrombosis due to impaired venous return and blood stasis. During difficult cannulations, the tourniquet may need to be released and reapplied to minimize distal ischemica

brief_summary:
The PhotonBlade 3 Smoke Evacuation device is a monopolar RF device coupled with illumination that is FDA approved and indicated for cutting and coagulation of soft tissue during surgical procedures and for removing smoke generated by electrosurgery when used in conjunction with an effective smoke evacuation system. The device includes a coated electrode at the distal end of a rotatable and extendable shaft (telescope) which delivers monopolar radiofrequency energy for cutting and coagulation of tissue. These devices enable the operator to remotely conduct an electrosurgical current from the output connector of an electrosurgical unit (ESU) to the operative site for the desired surgical effect. The integrated LED-based illumination allows the user to turn on or off the illumination. The integrated smoke evacuation tubing enables the user to evacuate smoke generated by electrosurgery when used in conjunction with an effective smoke evacuation system.

The Photon Blade 3 integrates localized surgical field illumination, simultaneous electrosurgical dissection, and active smoke evacuation. By improving visualization at the point of dissection and reducing smoke plume accumulation, surgeons perform more precise tissue dissection and hemostasis. The Photon Blade 3 device is FDA approved and being used in standard clinical care at Cleveland Clinic per its intended use. Utilization of the Photon Blade 3 expands feasibility of hidden scar lumpectomy approaches without compromising tissue handling. Cosmetic outcome after lumpectomy significantly influences patient satisfaction, body image, and quality of life. Reduced tissue trauma, optimized hemostasis, and improved control of the resection cavity translate into preservation of native breast contour, potentially leading to lower incidence of fat necrosis with less thermal injury, and more discrete scar placement.

The overall goal of this study is to assess the clinical performance and safety of the Photon Blade 3 illuminated electrosurgical device with integrated smoke evacuation, including patient reported outcomes, incorporation of oncoplastic techniques, and surgical field optimization. This study allows for the collection of data from cases where the device is already being used in standard clinical care in accordance with its FDA approved indication.
primary_outcomes: Degree of clinical performance assess at the time of surgery by the operative success rate and occurrence of intraoperative complications.
Postoperative complication rate assessed by the occurrence of pre-specified AE's at 3 days post-op, 2 weeks post-op, 45 days post-op and 90 days post-op.
title: Stryker Photon Blade 3 Outcomes

brief_summary:
The IMPACT-Ready Study is a multi-site, international short-term prospective natural history study to develop new outcome measures, clinical endpoints, and biomarkers for autism and related neurodevelopmental conditions. The primary objective is to systematically document over time the behavioral, medical, neurophysiological, and genetic presentation of children with profound autism and related neurodevelopmental conditions. Participants will be initially separated into two cohorts: those with a confirmed diagnosis of a monogenic disorder associated with profound autism, including ARID1B, GRIN2B, RNU4-2, SCN2A, SLC6A1, or other genes of interest (Cohort 1), or those with likely profound or profound autism without a definitive genetic cause for their autism at the time of enrollment who use few or no words to communicate, with significant cognitive impairments (Cohort 2).

All participants will complete a baseline visit, and a subset of participants will complete either 6-month or annual follow-up visits based on the results of their genetic testing and their age.

After whole genome sequencing and Fragile X testing at the baseline visit, Cohort 2 will be split into 2 groups: Cohort 2a (those with a definitive genetic cause for autism not identified) and Cohort 2b (those with the presence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant(s) in a neurodevelopmental gene other than one of the targeted genes of interest AND those that do not meet the criteria for profound/likely profound autism following baseline assessment).
title: IMPACT-Ready Study

brief_summary:
The research team hypothesizes that ceftazidime, in conjunction with vancomycin, is a safe and effective way to prevent surgical site infections in lumbar spinal surgery.

Objective 1: Evaluate the drain and serum concentrations of ceftazidime + vancomycin from 0-3 days postoperative. Hypothesis: The investigators hypothesize that intrawound ceftazidime will remain concentrated at the wound site, and there will be minimal absorption of ceftazidime into the circulatory system.

Hypothesis: The investigators hypothesize that intrawound ceftazidime, in conjunction with intrawound vancomycin, is a safe and effective way to reduce surgical site infections following lumbar spine surgery, while having little effect on construct fusion (e.g., pseudoarthrosis).

brief_summary:
This clinical trial will test whether a Cordyceps supplement improves lung function. The supplement is called Cordyceps sinensis mycelium Culture extract (Cs4). The study will include adults with pneumoconiosis, a lung disease caused by breathing in mineral dust. Researchers will also assess Cs4 safety.

The main questions are: (1) does Cs4 improve lung function compared with a placebo? (2) what health problems occur while participants take Cs4?

The study will include 84 adults aged 18 to 75 years. Their breathing condition must have been stable for at least three months. The study will take place at the School of Chinese Medicine, The University of Hong Kong.

Researchers will compare Cs4 with a placebo, a look-alike capsule containing no Cs4. Chance will determine which capsules each participant receives. Each participant has an equal chance of joining either group. Participants and researchers who assess them will not know which capsules participants receive.

Participants will: (1) take two capsules of Cs4 or placebo twice daily for 24 weeks; (2) record the capsules they take each day and return unused capsules at study visits; (3) attend clinic visits for breathing tests, a walking test, and blood tests; (4)answer questions about their breathing symptoms and daily life. (5) continue follow-up visits for 12 weeks after finishing the capsules.
primary_outcomes: Forced Expiratory Volume in One Second/ Forced Vital Capacity (FEV1/FVC) ratio

brief_summary:
General Objectives

1. To measure the effectiveness of the stress and coping mechanism training program that is meant to help nurses deal with occupational stress and at the same time provide healthcare services to Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus patients in the Hail Region.
2. To find out the impact of increased ability of nurses to cope with stress and its consequences on blood glucose levels and health of patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
3. To explore the connection between nurses' psychological state and quality of the care offered to diabetic patients in the region.
4. To examine the long-term effects of stress management techniques on the performance, emotional state, and engagement of nurses.
5. To explore how training in stress and coping mechanisms could affect the establishment of an empathic environment that would make the patients adhere to diabetes management programs.
6. To provide inputs into the elaboration of integrated healthcare programs that would take into consideration both psychological resilience of nurses and physiological stability of patients with diabetes and other chronic diseases.

Specific Objectives

1. To measure occupational stress experienced by the nurses before and after attending a training course on psychological stress and coping methods.
2. To determine the impact of the nurses' training program on patients' glucose control by measuring HbA1c.
3. To determine the relationship between the coping methods used by the nurses and adherence of patients to medications, diet and other self-management practices.
4. To find out the main coping methods used by the nurses which help to reduce stress and promote positive mood while providing nursing care to diabetic patients.
5. To learn patients' perception of the quality of care and communication after attending the nurses' training program on psychological stress and coping mechanisms.
6. To make recommendations about implementing the psychological training and stress management programs into the continuing professional education of nurses working in diabetes care units in Hail Region.

Research Questions

1. What is the efficiency of the program aimed at the development of coping and stress training of nurses working with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus patients in the Hail Region?
2. Is there any effect of improved stress management skills of nurses on the level of glycemic control of their patients, which is measured in terms of HbA1c values?
3. What are the connections between coping mechanisms of nurses and the adherence of their patients to prescribed treatment regimes?
4. What kind of coping strategies help nurses to feel better psychologically and be more satisfied with their job while working with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus patients?
5. How does the implementation of stress and coping mechanisms training affect patients' perception of the quality of the care provided and communication with nurses?
6. Can psychological training programs have an impact on health care delivery and patient outcomes among Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus patients in the Hail Region?

brief_summary: Emotional Freedom Technique (EFT) is a method used to manage negative emotions-such as anger, sadness, and anxiety-by applying fingertip stimulation to specific meridian points on the body. By reducing anxiety and fear, the use of EFT in the context of childbirth can increase maternal satisfaction. Since the fear of childbirth is a significant factor that negatively impacts the labor process, the reduction of such fear and anxiety through EFT strengthens the perception of satisfaction, leading to a more positive birth experience. Therefore, examining the relationship between the use of EFT during childbirth and maternal satisfaction is important from both clinical and psychosocial perspectives. Our study was designed to investigate the impact of the Emotional Freedom Technique on birth satisfaction.

brief_summary:
Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is a frequent reason for emergency department visits. Although most patients have a normal brain CT scan, this examination is still widely ordered, exposing patients to radiation, overloading imaging services and increasing care costs. The decision to perform a brain CT scan is usually based on validated clinical decision rules, such as the Canadian CT Head Rule (CCHR) or the New Orleans Criteria (NOC). However, several studies including a recent meta-analysis suggest significant CT overuse in the management of mTBI.

In recent years, biomarkers specific to brain injury mainly Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP) and Ubiquitin Carboxy-terminal Hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) have shown their ability to reliably rule out the presence of clinically significant intracranial injuries.

The combined use of GFAP and UCH-L1 has been recommended by the French Society of Anesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine (SFAR) and the French Society of Emergency Medicine (SFMU) in patients with mild traumatic brain injury at intermediate risk of intracranial bleeding, in order to limit the number of brain CT scans. Although prospective observational studies have evaluated the value of using these biomarkers, no study has evaluated their implementation in routine clinical practice.
interventions: Follow-up telephone call after one month
primary_outcomes: The proportion of patients who underwent GFAP and UCH-L1 testing, and in whom a brain CT scan was avoided following a negative result in accordance with current guidelines
title: The Use of GFAP and UCH-L1 Biomarkers in Clinical Practice for the Management of Mild Traumatic Brain Injury

brief_summary: This study compares two types of artificial implants used to replace a broken part of the elbow (the radial head) when the bone is too damaged to repair. One implant (press-fit) is designed to grip the bone tightly so bone grows into it and holds it in place. The other implant (loose-fit) has a smooth stem that sits loosely in the bone and is meant to move slightly. Both implants are already approved and widely used; doctors do not yet know if one works better than the other. People taking part are placed by chance into one of the two implant groups. The study will follow them for at least 2 years to see how far they can bend and straighten the elbow, how much pain they have, how well the elbow works in daily life, whether the implant stays in good position on X-rays, and whether any further surgery is needed.
title: Press-Fit vs Loose-Fit Radial Head Arthroplasty

brief_summary:
Nephrotic syndrome is a kidney disease that commonly affects children. It causes the kidneys to lose too much protein through urine. Corticosteroids (steroid medicines) are the main treatment, and most children respond well. However, some children do not improve with this treatment and develop steroid resistance.

One possible reason for this difference is a protein called P-glycoprotein (P-gp), which helps remove medicines from cells. When P-gp is more active, it may remove steroids from cells too quickly, reducing their effectiveness. The ABCB1 (MDR1) gene controls the production of this protein.

This study aims to investigate ABCB1 gene activity in children with nephrotic syndrome at different stages of the disease: at diagnosis, during remission, and in patients with steroid resistance. The goal is to determine whether measuring ABCB1 gene expression can help predict which children will respond to steroid treatment and which may develop steroid resistance.
title: THE EFFECT OF MDR1 IN NEPHORİC SENDROME

brief_summary:
This study evaluates the real-world effectiveness, safety, and immunogenicity of a single dose of the Vi-CRM197 typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) delivered through a mass vaccination campaign in selected districts of Madagascar. The study targets individuals aged 9 months to 45 years living in defined catchment areas with a high burden of typhoid fever.

The project integrates three components: a population census with geographic mapping, a vaccination campaign using a WHO-prequalified Vi-CRM197 TCV, and prospective surveillance for typhoid fever. Vaccine effectiveness will be assessed by comparing the incidence of blood culture-confirmed Salmonella Typhi infection among vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals during follow-up. Additional outcomes include clinically suspected typhoid fever, severe disease, vaccine safety, immunogenicity, antibiotic use and consumption, and carriage of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) markers.

The study aims to generate real-world evidence to inform public health decision-making regarding typhoid vaccine introduction and its broader impact on disease burden and antimicrobial resistance in endemic settings.

brief_summary:
\*\*Study Objective\*\*

The aim of this randomized controlled trial is to evaluate the effects of manual lymphatic drainage massage and classical massage on autonomic and hemodynamic responses in community-dwelling older adults aged 60 years and older. The study is expected to contribute to understanding the effects of massage interventions on autonomic and hemodynamic responses and to the development of evidence-based, non-pharmacological interventions supporting older adults' health.

\*\*Study Hypotheses\*\*

Primary Hypothesis (H01): The effects of a single 15-minute session of manual lymphatic drainage massage and classical massage on cardiac autonomic function in community-dwelling older adults differ from those observed in the delayed-intervention control group.

Secondary Hypothesis (H02): The effects of a single 15-minute session of manual lymphatic drainage massage and classical massage on hemodynamic responses in community-dwelling older adults differ from those observed in the delayed-intervention control group.

\*\*Study Design and Procedures\*\*

A total of 75 participants will be randomly assigned to one of three groups: manual lymphatic drainage massage, classical massage, or a delayed-intervention control group.

Participants in the manual lymphatic drainage massage group will receive a single 15-minute session involving gentle, rhythmic massage techniques applied to the neck and supraclavicular regions. Participants in the classical massage group will receive a single 15-minute session involving traditional massage techniques applied to the neck and shoulders. Participants in the delayed-intervention control group will rest for 15 minutes without receiving massage.

Heart rate variability (HRV), heart rate, and blood pressure will be measured before and immediately after the 15-minute massage or rest period in all three groups. HRV measures the natural variation in time between heartbeats and provides information about the regulation of heart function by the autonomic nervous system.

Changes in these measurements will be compared among the three groups to evaluate short-term autonomic and hemodynamic responses.

After completion of the study, participants in the delayed-intervention control group will be offered a massage intervention based on the study findings.
conditions: Autonomic and Hemodynamic Responses in Older Adults
primary_outcomes: Change in Heart Rate Variability (LF/HF Ratio)
title: Effects of Manual Lymphatic Drainage and Classical Massage on Autonomic and Hemodynamic Responses in Community-Dwelling Older Adults

brief_summary: This is a 12-month randomized controlled trial designed to evaluate the effectiveness of a comprehensive self-applied lifestlye intervention for weight loss, based on portion control. The control group will receive standard guidelines for healthy living, including diet and physical activity. Both groups will attend 4 clinical investigation days, 2 group sessions and will receive periodic telephone support. The primary outcome will be the change in waist circumference from baseline, assessed at 3, 9 and 12 months. Other measurements will include body composition, fasting biochemical parameters, eating behaviour, gut microbiota, functional magnetic resonance, portion size norms, intervention adherence and acceptance. The study will test the hypothesis that a comprehensive intervention focused on portion control can promote changes in eating habits and reduce waist circumference over 12 months compared with receving standard healthy living advice (active control group).

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if a nurse-led self-management support program, called BRIDGE-SM, reduces unplanned hospital readmissions and emergency department visits in adults having planned (elective) coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. It will also learn if the program improves heart self-care and lowers depression, anxiety, and stress after surgery.

The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does BRIDGE-SM lower the number of patients who are readmitted to hospital or visit the emergency department within 45 days after discharge?
* Does BRIDGE-SM improve patients' heart self-care at 45 days after discharge?
* Does BRIDGE-SM lower depression, anxiety, and stress at 45 days after discharge?

Researchers will compare patients who receive BRIDGE-SM plus usual hospital care with patients who receive usual hospital care alone. They will also compare deaths from any cause within 45 days after hospital discharge between the two groups to check safety.

Participants in the BRIDGE-SM group will:

* Attend one face-to-face education session (20 to 40 minutes) with a specialist cardiac nurse at the preoperative assessment clinic, and receive an Arabic educational video and electronic leaflets by WhatsApp
* Attend one face-to-face discharge session (20 to 45 minutes) on the day they leave hospital, and receive a printed Arabic self-management booklet
* Receive four scheduled phone calls from the nurse on Days 3, 14, 21, and 30 after discharge
* Be able to contact the nurse by WhatsApp or phone with questions at any time during the 30 days after discharge

All participants will complete questionnaires on heart self-care and on depression, anxiety, and stress at 45 days after discharge, two weeks after the nurse follow-up period ends. Participants in the usual care group will be offered a nurse consultation after their follow-up ends.
primary_outcomes: Number of Participants With Unplanned Healthcare Utilization (Unplanned Hospital Readmission or Emergency Department Visit)
title: Nurse-Led Self-Management Support After Coronary Artery Bypass Surgery

This study evaluates TXN10128 in combination with either irinotecan (a topoisomerase I inhibitor) or a TROP2-directed antibody-drug conjugate (TROP2 ADC) in participants with advanced or metastatic NSCLC with confirmed EGFR mutations.

The study consists of three cohorts. It enrolls participants who have progressed after prior treatment with a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) and platinum-based doublet chemotherapy.

Part B enrolls participants who are currently receiving TROP2 ADC therapy or whose disease has progressed following such therapy (with no restriction on the number of prior lines).

In Part C, participants who are naïve to TROP2 ADC therapy and have received no more than three prior lines of systemic anticancer therapy will be enrolled. A safety run-in will first be conducted to confirm the safety of the combination with a TROP2 ADC. Based on the results, the Safety Review Committee (SRC) will select the recommended dose for expansion phase, which will follow Simon's two-stage design.
title: Phase 1b/2 to Evaluate the Safety, Tolerability, and Efficacy of TXN10128 in Combination With TOPO-I Inhibitor-based Therapies (Irinotecan or TROP2 ADC) in Advanced or Metastatic EGFR Mutated NSCLC

brief_summary: Shoulder arthroscopy is often performed with the patient in an upright beach-chair position. The main outcome is the total cerebral desaturation burden, measured as the area below 80% of each participant's baseline cerebral oxygen saturation during monitoring. brief_summary: HIV rapidly infects the nervous system resulting in chronic infection that persists even when blood HIV is undetectable. The resulting inflammation causes progressive neuronal damage leading to cognitive decline in up to 50% of people living with HIV. The damage to the nervous system is due in part to a loss of natural processes that protect the brain. There are currently no effective treatments. A novel new drug, LM11A-31, has been shown to restore the protective processes thereby shifting the balance from degenerative to protective activity. Beneficial effects have been seen in patients with Alzheimer's disease and research indicates that it should have similar beneficial effects in people living with HIV. The proposed study will establish the safety and tolerability of LM11A-31 treatment in a small cohort of stable virally-suppressed participants with HIV and mild neurocognitive impairment. The focus will be on individuals 50-75 years of age who are most vulnerable for cognitive decline. To provide sufficient time to stabilize brain activity, participants will take tablets twice daily over a period of 48 weeks. The main focus of the trial will be on safety but will also be supplemented with exploratory characterization of biomarkers to confirm a reduction in degeneration as well as to provide early identification of individuals at risk for neurodegeneration. These studies are expected to show that LM11A-31 is safe to use in people living with HIV and to provide preliminary data indicating protection from neuronal damage and cognitive decline.

brief_summary:
Recurrent respiratory tract infections (RRTIs) are common among preschool children and can affect children's health and place considerable caregiving demands on their families. Parents play an important role in recognizing respiratory symptoms, providing appropriate home care, and seeking timely medical attention. Improving parental health literacy and providing accessible health management support may help families manage recurrent respiratory infections.

This study evaluated RESPIRE, a robot-assisted ecological momentary intervention designed to support respiratory symptom monitoring and parental management of RRTIs in preschool children.

The study used a two-arm, parallel-group, cluster-randomized controlled trial design involving two public kindergartens in Dingxi, Gansu Province, China. Eligible preschool children with RRTIs and one primary caregiver for each child were included. The two kindergartens were randomly assigned to either the intervention group or the control group.

The intervention group received an eight-week RESPIRE program combining kindergarten-based robot-assisted health screening with a mobile application for parents. The program included daily respiratory health monitoring, personalized health guidance, interactive health education, and online peer support. The control group received routine kindergarten health care and reported children's respiratory symptoms daily.

The primary outcome was parental health literacy, assessed at baseline, week 4, and week 8. Secondary outcomes included the frequency of respiratory tract infections, the proportion of days with respiratory symptoms, parenting sense of competence, parenting stress, intervention adherence, system usability, and participant satisfaction.

The study aimed to evaluate whether the RESPIRE program could improve parental health literacy and support the management of recurrent respiratory tract infections among preschool children.
title: Robot-Assisted Intervention for Recurrent Respiratory Infections in Preschoolers

brief_summary:
This study aims to determine the effect of motivational interviewing administered to the male partner on the female partner's perception of spousal support and infertility-related stress in couples undergoing infertility treatment.

H1 1: Motivational counselling provided to the male partner during the infertility treatment process reduces the woman's level of infertility-related stress during the treatment process. H1 2: Motivational counselling provided to the male partner during the infertility treatment process increases the level of spousal support perceived by the woman.

The study will be conducted using a randomised controlled experimental design. In addition to the routine nursing roles at the clinic, men in the experimental group will undergo structured motivational interviewing. The control group, which will not receive motivational interviewing, will instead undergo the routine nursing roles at the clinic. Independent Variable: Motivational interviewing administered to men during the infertility treatment process Dependent Variable: The woman's perception of spousal support and infertility-related stress The research will be conducted as a randomised controlled experimental study. Infertility is defined by the World Health Organisation as problems with the male or female reproductive system where pregnancy cannot be achieved despite regular, unprotected sexual intercourse for a year or longer. Motivational interviewing is a specific, short-term therapy method that is easy to implement and learn, used to help individuals understand their problems, believe in change, and take action. Its effectiveness has been confirmed in numerous studies, particularly in individuals who are reluctant or indecisive about change. Being an evidence-based method, it enhances reliability in practice. The Motivational Interviewing technique developed by Miller and Rollnick aims to support individuals in gaining self-insight and finding solutions to change their behaviour. Its suitability for different areas of application demonstrates a broad potential for use. Although motivational interviewing has limited use in the field of infertility, it is planned to be applied to men in infertile couples to increase the level of support the man provides to his partner and to reduce the woman's stress related to infertility.
primary_outcomes: Change in Total Score on The COMPI Fertility Problem Stress Scales Among Women
Change in Spousal Support Scale Total Score Among Women
title: The Effect of Motivational Interviewing Applied to Men During the Infertility Treatment Process on the Perception of Spouse Support and Infertility Stress in Women

brief_summary: This is an observational, longitudinal study with a control group, with the general objective of analysing the pattern of response of prefrontal cortex activity during motor and cognitive tasks in individuals with and without Parkinson's disease (PD) over 12 months. Prefrontal activity was recorded with a portable hemoencephalography (HEG) device placed on the forehead, in rest-task-rest blocks, while participants performed the Box and Block Test, the Nine-Hole Peg Test, the Trail Making Test (parts A and B) and spiral and sinusoid drawings. The assessments were repeated in up to 12 sessions, planned approximately monthly, and the tasks were video-recorded showing only the hands. Participants with PD were also assessed with the MDS-UPDRS Part III, the Hoehn \& Yahr scale and the PDQ-39 at the first and last sessions. Information that can identify the participants will be removed from the database before storage in a repository. The results will contribute to understanding how prefrontal activity relates to motor and cognitive performance in PD and how it changes over time.

brief_summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to learn whether a hybrid parasternal intercostal plane block (HPIP) reduces pain after heart surgery performed through a median sternotomy in adults. The main question it aims to answer is:

\- Does HPIP lower pain scores during coughing 12 hours after surgery compared with no block?

Researchers will also compare pain at rest, opioid use, time to first rescue pain medication, time to removal of the breathing tube, length of ICU and hospital stay, and block-related complications such as pneumothorax.

HPIP combines two ultrasound-guided chest wall nerve blocks: a superficial parasternal intercostal plane block (S-PIP) on the left side and a deep parasternal intercostal plane block (D-PIP) on the right side. This approach aims to keep the potential pain-relief benefits of the deep block while limiting its risks (such as pneumothorax and injury to the internal mammary artery) to the right side only, away from the left internal mammary artery commonly harvested for coronary bypass grafting.

Participants will:

* Be randomly assigned (1:1) to receive HPIP or no block after induction of general anesthesia and before skin incision
* Receive the same standard multimodal pain management after surgery, including scheduled acetaminophen, fentanyl IV patient-controlled analgesia, and rescue pain medication as needed
* Have their pain and recovery assessed by staff who do not know their group assignment
primary_outcomes: Pain score on coughing at 12 hours after surgery

brief_summary:
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide, and many patients do not respond adequately to available treatments. Plasticity, the ability of the brain and mind to change, is thought to be a crucial process in the transition from depression to wellbeing, but methods to measure it are limited. The Network Theory of Plasticity proposes that the weaker the connections among the elements of a system (for example, the symptoms of a patient or the regions of the brain), the higher its plasticity. Earlier analyses of large clinical datasets (STAR\*D and CO-MED) supported this idea at the population level.

PlastNet is an observational study that aims to validate this approach at the individual level. Two hundred adults (18-70 years) with nonpsychotic MDD recruited at IRCCS Ospedale San Raffaele will undergo resting-state brain MRI, blood sampling and clinical assessments at baseline, and clinical assessments again after four weeks. No treatment is assigned by the study.

The investigators hypothesize that lower baseline functional connectivity in the brain is associated with a greater reduction in depressive symptoms over four weeks. The study will also investigate whether blood-based multi-omic profiles (genomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic) can identify biological signatures of plasticity. The results could help clinicians tailor treatments to each patient's level of plasticity.
primary_outcomes: Change in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS-17) total score from baseline to week 4
title: Predicting Transitions From Depression to Wellbeing Through a Network-based Operationalization of Plasticity

brief_summary:
Gender-based violence is a widespread public health problem and a serious violation of human rights. Nurses play a key role in identifying and supporting women experiencing violence; however, nursing students often report feeling insufficiently prepared to address these situations in clinical practice. Although simulation-based learning is widely recommended for developing communication, assessment, and decision-making skills, evidence comparing active participation with structured observational learning in gender-based violence education remains limited.

This study aims to compare the effectiveness of active participation in a standardized patient simulation and structured observational learning on nursing students' knowledge of gender-based violence and their satisfaction with the learning experience.

A parallel-group randomized controlled trial will be conducted at a public university in Barcelona, Spain. A total of 122 first-year nursing students will be randomly assigned to either an active participation group or a structured observational learning group. Before the simulation experience, participants will complete the Multidimensional Scale of Dating Violence 2.0 to assess previous exposure to dating violence. Following a theoretical class session and a pre-briefing, students will engage in a high-fidelity simulation scenario involving a standardized patient experiencing gender-based violence. Participants in the intervention group will actively perform the simulation, while those in the control group will observe the scenario using a structured observation guide. Both groups will subsequently participate in the same facilitated debriefing session.

Knowledge acquisition will be assessed immediately before and after the intervention using a 14-item ad hoc knowledge checklist. Satisfaction with the simulation experience will be measured using the Spanish Satisfaction Scale Questionnaire with High-Fidelity Clinical Simulation (CS-SCAF). The study will evaluate changes in knowledge and satisfaction associated with active versus observational participation in simulation-based training on gender-based violence.
primary_outcomes: Change in Knowledge of Gender-Based Violence
title: Learning Through Observation or Participation in Gender-Based Violence Simulation: A Randomized Trial

brief_summary: Objective: To explore whether a 12-week basketball-based cognitive-motor dual-task training (CMDT) improves adolescents' personal growth initiative and functional components of AI dependence, and to examine its effects on critical thinking disposition. Methods: This 12-week randomized controlled trial recruited 106 adolescents aged 18-19 years, who were randomly assigned to either the CMDT group or the control group. The CMDT group received basketball training embedded with cognitive tasks, while the control group participated in conventional basketball training with matched exercise volume. Assessments were conducted at baseline (week 0), mid-intervention (week 6), and post-intervention (week 12) using the Personal Growth Initiative Scale-II (PGIS-II), Critical Thinking Disposition Scale (CTDS), and Conversational AI Dependence Scale (CAIDS-20). A 2 × 3 mixed repeated-measures analysis of variance was adopted to test the main effects of group, time, and group-by-time interaction effects.
title: Basketbal Based Motor Cognitive Training Promotes Adolescents' Personal Growth Initiative and Reduces Reliance on AI

The goal of this clinical trial is to evaluate whether the implementation of a real-time prognostic model can effectively identify and prevent blood clots among hospitalized patients. The main questions it aims to answer is:

1. Can the prognostic model reduce rates of hospital-acquired blood clots (also known as hospital-acquired venous thromboembolisms)?
2. Is the prognostic model an effective tool for initiating timely and appropriate preventive treatment (i.e., thromboprophylaxis)?

Researchers will compare the intervention arm with the control arm (standard of care) to determine whether the intervention reduces rates of blood clots and improves initiation of preventive treatment.

The intervention (clinical decision support that displays the prognostic model's output) will be implemented by displaying a risk score in clinicians' workflow in the electronic health record (EHR) to notify clinicians of patients who are at higher risk for sustaining a blood clot. The intervention will not dictate patient care and clinicians will continue to use their clinical knowledge and judgment in their clinical decision-making.

This study aims to investigate the acute effects of L-theanine, L-tyrosine, and their combination on cognitive performance and archery performance in trained archers. The study will use a randomized, placebo-controlled, five-condition crossover design involving 21 healthy male archers aged 18 years or older.

Participants will complete five experimental conditions: placebo, L-theanine supplementation (6 mg/kg), L-tyrosine supplementation (50 mg/kg), combined L-theanine and L-tyrosine supplementation, and a no-supplement control condition. Supplements will be administered 60 minutes before performance assessments, with at least 72 hours between experimental sessions.

Cognitive performance will be assessed using the Stroop Test, while archery performance will be evaluated through indoor target shooting at 18 meters. Mood states and perceived exertion will also be assessed using the BRUMS questionnaire and Borg CR-10 scale, respectively.

The study will examine whether these supplementation conditions produce different acute responses in cognitive function and archery performance.

This randomized clinical trial aims to investigate whether combining virtual reality with stationary cycling produces different effects on motor and cognitive function compared with stationary cycling alone in people with Parkinson's disease.

Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups: a control group performing stationary cycling and an intervention group performing stationary cycling while using a virtual reality headset. The intervention will consist of 12 sessions over six weeks, with two sessions per week. Each session will last 40 minutes, including 5 minutes for vital sign assessment before exercise, 30 minutes of cycling, and 5 minutes for vital sign reassessment after exercise.

Assessments will be conducted before the intervention, immediately after the six-week program, and at follow-up. The study will examine whether adding virtual reality to stationary cycling may be a useful approach for rehabilitation in people with Parkinson's disease.

The goal of this clinical trial is to investigate the effects of meal sequence(the order in which carbohydrates/starches and non-starchy vegetables are consumed) and eating speed(slow or fast) on postprandial blood glucose response in healthy young adults (n=22) aged 20-25 years. The main questions it aims to answer are:

* Does consuming carbohydrate-containing foods before or after non-starchy vegetables influence postprandial blood glucose response?
* Does eating a standardized breakfast slowly (over approximately 20 minutes) or quickly (over approximately 10 minutes) affect postprandial blood glucose response?
* Do meal sequence and eating speed together influence postprandial glycemic response? Researchers will compare four breakfast conditions combining two meal sequences (carbohydrate-first and non-starchy vegetable-first) with two eating speeds (slow and fast) to determine their individual and combined effects on postprandial metabolic responses.

Participants will:

* Consume a standardized, isocaloric Western-style breakfast under four different experimental conditions.
* Consume the breakfast in the assigned food order and within the specified eating duration during each experimental visit.
* Attend four experimental visits in a randomized order, with a washout period between visits.
* Provide blood samples before and at 30, 60, 90, and 120 minutes after breakfast consumption to assess blood glucose levels.
* Undergo assessment of serum insulin and triglyceride responses according to the study protocol.

primary_outcomes: Proportion of participants with HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL in Patient living with HIV(PLWH) with virologic failure (VF) and virologically unsuppressed (VU). Analyzed to the FDA snapshot
title: Bictegravir Efficacy With 1st INSTI Generation Failure History

brief_summary: The goal of this clinical trial is to learn which of two hands-on ankle treatments works better for amateur footballers aged 18 to 35 with unstable ankles, meaning ankles that keep "giving way" after an old sprain. The study will find out which treatment better improves how far the ankle bends upward, balance while standing and reaching on one leg, and hopping on the injured leg compared with the healthy leg. Researchers will compare Maitland mobilization, where the therapist gently and rhythmically moves the ankle joint while the participant lies still, with Mulligan mobilization, where the therapist holds the ankle bones in a guided position while the participant bends the ankle. Participants will receive one of the two treatments, followed by ankle strengthening exercises, 3 times a week for 8 weeks. They will complete simple tests of ankle movement, balance and hopping at the start, at week 4 and at week 8.
lead_sponsor: University of Management and Technology Lahore
primary_outcomes: Ankle Dorsiflexion Range of Motion: Weight-Bearing Lunge Test (WBLT)
Single-Leg Hop Tests, Limb Symmetry Index (LSI)
title: Comparative Effects of Two Hands-On Ankle Treatments on Range of Motion, Dynamic Balance and Hop Performance in Amateur Footballers With Ankle Instability

brief_summary: Doctors will use a mHealth application to evaluate the risk of thrombosis and bleeding in patients with cancer.
primary_outcomes: Proprtion of patients with appropriate thromboprophylaxis use
title: Use of mHealth Application and Education to Increase Appropriateness of Thromboprophylaxis in Patients With Cancer

brief_summary: The goal of this study is to (1) determine the feasibility and acceptability of a telehealth-delivered exercise intervention (including resistance and aerobic training) during neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) for women with high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) and to (2) determine the effect of exercise on changes in immune function, inflammation, and treatment response.
title: Identifying Mediators of Exercise-induced Tumor Microenvironment Remodeling to Enhance Primary Chemotherapy Response (IMPROVE-Ovarian)

brief_summary: Colonoscopies are performed during two different time slots: in the morning and in the afternoon. The objective is to evaluate which time of day offers a more comfortable experience regarding post-procedure pain and which results in more effective bowel preparation, thereby ensuring higher-quality procedure outcomes.
primary_outcomes: Patient Pain Level as Assessed by Visual Analog Scale (VAS)
title: Morning vs Afternoon Colonoscopy: Effects on Quality and Postprocedural Pain

brief_summary: This is a two-arm, open-label, randomized interventional study involving women newly diagnosed with breast cancer.
primary_outcomes: Feasibility of conducting a future clinical trial
title: Patient-Centered Clinical Trial Navigation: Addressing Gender Disparity in Clinical Trial Participation

brief_summary: This randomized controlled trial aims to investigate whether interrupting prolonged sitting with physical activity breaks can improve executive function in university students and to explore the potential underlying neural mechanisms. Participants will complete three experimental conditions in a randomized, within-subject crossover design: uninterrupted sitting (control condition), sitting interrupted by physical activity breaks, and a moderate-intensity exercise condition (exercise control). Executive function will be assessed before and after each condition using a computerized Stroop task. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) will simultaneously monitor changes in cortical oxygenation, particularly in the prefrontal and parietal regions. The study hypothesizes that interrupting prolonged sitting with physical activity breaks will acutely improve executive function, particularly inhibitory control, compared with uninterrupted sitting. It is also expected that changes in cortical oxygenation may be associated with improvements in cognitive performance.
title: Breaks in Sedentary Behaviour and Executive Function

brief_summary: This is a single-site observational, before/after cohort study comparing intermittent blood pressure measurement using to continuous noninvasive blood pressure measurement. The study is designed to determine the impact of the use of continuous noninvasive blood pressure monitoring on the incidence of hypotension in high-risk patients undergoing sedation for upper or lower endoscopic procedures.
title: Continuous BP Monitoring During Sedation for Endoscopy

brief_summary: This study is being done to look at how well zenagamtide lowers blood sugar levels and body weight in people with type 2 diabetes when compared to placebo. Participants will either get zenagamtide, the treatment being tested or placebo, a treatment that has no active medicine in it. Which treatment participants get is decided by chance. Zenagamtide is a new medicine that doctors cannot prescribe yet, but it has been tested in humans before.
title: A Research Study Investigating How Well Zenagamtide Lowers Blood Sugar and Body Weight Compared to Placebo in People With Type 2 Diabetes Treated With Diet and Exercise

brief_summary: This study tests whether adding aerobic exercise to diaphragmatic breathing helps overweight and obese children with primary nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting) more than diaphragmatic breathing alone. Children aged 6 to 12 years who wet the bed at least 3 times a week are randomly assigned to one of three groups: aerobic exercise plus diaphragmatic breathing, diaphragmatic breathing alone, or a waiting-list control group. The program lasts 12 weeks. The main outcomes are the number of bedwetting episodes per week and sleep quality. Body mass index and quality of life are also compared.
primary_outcomes: Frequency of nocturnal enuresis episodes per week
Sleep quality measured with the Child and Adolescent Sleep Checklist (CASC) total score
title: Aerobic Exercise Added to Diaphragmatic Breathing for Nocturnal Enuresis in Overweight and Obese Children

A total of 59 neonates were randomized to continuous KMC (n=30) or intermittent KMC (n=29). The primary outcome was weight gain. primary_outcomes: Weight gain in low birth weight neonates
title: Continuous vs Intermittent Kangaroo Mother Care and Weight Gain in Low Birth Weight Infants

brief_summary: This study will evaluate whether a nurse-led heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback programme supported by a low-cost wearable sensor reduces autonomic dysregulation and perceived stress in informal caregivers of people with dementia. Participants will be prospectively allocated, without randomization, at the day-care-centre level. Before enrolment, the six centres will be characterised according to centre size, estimated number of eligible caregivers and expected recruitment volume, and arranged into three approximately matched pairs. One centre in each pair will implement CARE-COHERENCE and the other will serve as a concurrent comparison centre under a pre-specified operational implementation plan. Follow-up will continue for 12 months.
lead_sponsor: Instituto de Investigación Marqués de Valdecilla
